GLM-5.1 appears to score 58.4% on SWE-Bench Pro, which several sources describe as a state-of-the-art result at release and ahead of GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on that benchmark.[3][4][5]

## Benchmark result

The clearest claim comes from Z.AI’s GLM-5.1 documentation, which says GLM-5.1 achieved 58.4 on SWE-Bench Pro.  Independent writeups repeat that figure and frame it as the top published result at the time of launch.[4][5][3]

One source breaks out the comparison more specifically, stating GLM-5.1 at 58.4 versus GPT-5.4 at 57.7 and Claude Opus 4.6 at 54.2.  Another source also says it beat Gemini 3.1 Pro, though the exact Gemini figure is not consistently shown across the results I found.[5][3][4]

## What that means

SWE-Bench Pro is presented as a benchmark for difficult software engineering tasks based on real GitHub issues, so a strong score there suggests the model is good at repository-level debugging and implementation work rather than just short coding answers.  In that context, GLM-5.1’s result is being used to position it as a serious agentic coding model, not just a chatbot with coding ability.[3][4][5]

Several sources also tie that score to long-horizon execution, claiming GLM-5.1 can work autonomously on tasks for up to 8 hours and use a 200K context window.  That does not prove real-world superiority in every workflow, but it helps explain why it may perform well on engineering-style benchmarks.[6][5]

## Important caveat

The strongest evidence here is still partly vendor-led because the main benchmark claim comes from the model’s own documentation, while many other pages are summaries or commentary repeating the same release narrative.  I did also find the official SWE-bench leaderboard site, but the search snippet alone did not expose the GLM-5.1 entry directly, so I cannot independently verify the exact leaderboard row from that page with complete confidence from the material available here.[1][4][5][3]

## Practical takeaway

If you are asking, “How did GLM-5.1 do on SWE-Bench Pro?”, the answer is: reportedly 58.4%, and sources around its release described that as the best published score at the time.  If you want, I can next compare GLM-5.1 specifically against GPT-5.4 or explain what SWE-Bench Pro actually measures in plain language.[4][5][3]

Claude Opus 4.8 is reported at 69.2% on SWE-Bench Pro, with Opus 4.7 at 64.3%, according to multiple sources summarizing Anthropic’s launch materials.[1][3][5]

## Reported score

The most consistent number across the sources I found is 69.2% for Claude Opus 4.8 on SWE-Bench Pro.  Those same sources say this was a 4.9-point improvement over Opus 4.7’s 64.3%.[3][5][1]

One source also compares Opus 4.8 with other frontier models on the same benchmark, listing GPT-5.5 at 58.6% and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 54.2%.  Another source repeats that same ranking and says Opus 4.8 was ahead of both on SWE-Bench Pro.[5][3]

## How to interpret it

SWE-Bench Pro is described as the harder SWE-bench variant, built around real repository-level software engineering tasks rather than short coding prompts.  That matters because higher performance there is usually taken as evidence of stronger debugging, patching, and multi-file code-change ability.[1][3][5]

A third-party writeup says Anthropic measured the 69.2% result using a full agent setup that could inspect repositories, run commands, test fixes, and iterate.  So the headline score reflects a best-case benchmark configuration rather than a plain one-shot chat answer.[1]

## Caveat

The number appears well corroborated across commentary and benchmark explainers, but the sources I have here are still mostly secondary reports citing Anthropic’s published materials rather than a directly inspected original benchmark table.  So I’d treat 69.2% as the currently reported figure, with good but not perfect independent verification from the material available here.[3][5][1]

## Context

One search result from the SWE-bench leaderboard site shows Claude Opus 4.6 at 75.60, which does not line up cleanly with the 69.2% Pro figure and likely reflects a different leaderboard setting or benchmark slice.  Because of that mismatch, the safest answer to your exact query is simply that Claude Opus 4.8 is being reported at 69.2% on SWE-Bench Pro.[8][5][3][1]

Would you like a side-by-side table for GLM-5.1 vs Claude Opus 4.8 on SWE-Bench Pro based only on the figures gathered here?

entries.answer:
GLM-5.1 scores about 58.4% on SWE-Bench Pro, while Claude Opus 4.8 scores about 69.2%, so Opus 4.8 is reported higher on this benchmark.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

## SWE-Bench Pro scores

| Model              | SWE-Bench Pro score (%) | Source context                                                                 | Notes                                                                                     |
|--------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| GLM-5.1            | 58.4                    | Reported in Z.AI docs and multiple benchmark articles. [1][2][3]   | First open-weight model to take #1 on SWE-Bench Pro at its release, beating earlier GPT/Claude/Gemini results then. [1][2][3] |
| Claude Opus 4.8    | 69.2                    | Reported in benchmark explainers summarizing Anthropic’s launch numbers. [4][5][6] | About +4.9 points over Opus 4.7 (64.3%), positioned as a new state-of-the-art closed model on SWE-Bench Pro. [4][5] |

## How to read this

The GLM-5.1 figure comes mainly from Z.AI’s documentation plus independent blog writeups, all agreeing on 58.4%.  The Claude Opus 4.8 figure comes from several third-party benchmark explainers that all quote Anthropic’s 69.2% number and the 64.3% baseline for Opus 4.7.[2][3][4][5][6][1]

One important nuance is that GLM-5.1 is open-weight and MIT-licensed, so its 58.4% is notable for an open model, whereas Opus 4.8 is proprietary, which may matter if you care about local or self-hosted deployment.  Also, both scores are measured in agent-style setups (tools, repo access, iteration), so they reflect full-system capability on long software tasks, not single-shot prompts.[3][4][5][1][2]

Are you mainly choosing between these two for local, self-hosted coding agents, or are you also fine using a closed cloud API like Anthropic’s?

GPT-5.5 is reported at 58.6% on SWE-Bench Pro in OpenAI’s launch page, which places it slightly above GPT-5.4’s 57.7% but below Claude Opus 4.7’s 64.3% in the same published comparison.[1]

## Reported score

The most direct source is OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 announcement, which states that GPT-5.5 reaches 58.6% on SWE-Bench Pro.  The same page includes a comparison row showing GPT-5.4 at 57.7%, Claude Opus 4.7 at 64.3%, and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 54.2% on the same benchmark.[1]

A third-party explainer reproduces the same table and says Claude kept the lead on SWE-Bench Pro versus GPT-5.5 by 5.7 points.  Another commentary source also repeats the 58.6% figure and notes that GPT-5.5 was nominally behind Opus 4.7 on this benchmark.[2][3]

## Important nuance

There is now a major naming complication around SWE-Bench Pro, because newer leaderboard materials from Scale describe a harder public dataset where top models are around 23% rather than near 60% or 70%.  That suggests the older 58.6% figure and the newer public leaderboard numbers may refer to different evaluation setups, benchmark versions, or reporting conventions rather than a single directly comparable scoreboard.[4][1]

Because of that mismatch, the safest answer to your exact question is that GPT-5.5 is reported at 58.6% on SWE-Bench Pro in OpenAI’s own benchmark table.  I would avoid treating that number as automatically interchangeable with every later “SWE-Bench Pro” leaderboard you may see.[4][1]

## Position versus others

Using the same table from OpenAI, GPT-5.5 sits above GPT-5.4 by 0.9 points and above Gemini 3.1 Pro by 4.4 points, but below Claude Opus 4.7 by 5.7 points.  Relative to the earlier number we discussed for GLM-5.1 at 58.4%, GPT-5.5 is essentially tied, at least based on the reported figures gathered here.[5][1]
